Today you start a short research note on the Nebraska yield data, in a new file, `analysis/note.qmd`, written by the AI from your decisions. This worksheet holds your decisions, your requests and your checks; the note itself is a separate file.

The note goes to a journal that asks for a Word file. A coauthor has sent you a reference file, `2-4-references.bib`, saying: "These are the three papers to cite. My AI assistant made the file for me."

**Rules:**

A. Decide the claims and what supports each **before** you ask the AI.

B. Keep the requests you actually sent in this file, with the blanks filled in.

C. The AI never writes a reference. It may only cite keys that are already in the `.bib` file.

D. You judge the note by reading the rendered output, in HTML and in Word.

# Task 2: Set up the note

**My request to the AI.** Fill in every `<...>`, then send it:

```text
Create a Quarto article at analysis/note.qmd for a journal that asks
for a Word file. Title "<title>"; author <your name and affiliation>;
an abstract I will write. Outputs: docx and html. References from
analysis/2-4-references.bib. No code in the docx output; code shown in
the html output. Headings, empty for now: Introduction, Data, Results.
Write the sentence for each chunk as a comment on the chunk's first
line, starting with #, so it shows with the code in the HTML version
and stays out of the Word version.

Put the code in my Quarto document analysis/note.qmd, under the
heading "Data", as R code chunks. Above each chunk, write one
plain-English sentence saying what it does and why. Build every path
with here::here(); no setwd(), no absolute paths. Print each check on
its own line as "name of check: expected X, got Y". Render the document
to HTML.
```

**Did it render? Does the HTML show the title, your name and the three headings?**

Your answer:

# Task 3: A numbered figure and table

**My request to the AI.** Fill in every `<...>` from Task 1, then send it. Send it twice, once for each claim, or put both in one request.

```text
In analysis/note.qmd, add a <figure or table> of <what it shows>,
labelled <fig- or tbl- label>, with the caption "<caption>". It
supports the sentence "<the claim>", which you add right after it,
referring to it with @<label>. The data is data/2-1-nebraska-yield.csv.
Check the number of rows read (I expect <number>). Write the sentence
for each chunk as a comment on the chunk's first line, starting with #,
so it shows with the code in the HTML version and stays out of the Word
version.

Put the code in my Quarto document analysis/note.qmd, under the
heading "Results", as R code chunks. Above each chunk, write one
plain-English sentence saying what it does and why. Build every path
with here::here(); no setwd(), no absolute paths. Print each check on
its own line as "name of check: expected X, got Y". Render the document
to HTML.
```

**In the HTML: does each sentence say "Figure 1" or "Table 1", not `?@`? Does each figure or table show what its sentence claims?**

# Task 4: Citations

Your coauthor wants these three sentences in the Introduction:

1. "Corn yields fall sharply on days hotter than about 29 degrees Celsius."
2. "As yields in the U.S. Midwest have risen, they have also become more sensitive to drought."
3. "Irrigation narrows the gap between yields in wet and dry years in Nebraska."

**My request to the AI:**

```text
In analysis/note.qmd, under the heading "Introduction", add these three
sentences, each with a citation: sentence 1 cites <key>, sentence 2
cites <key>, sentence 3 cites <key>.
<paste the three sentences>
Cite only keys already in analysis/2-4-references.bib; add no entries
to it, and change none. Then render the document to HTML.
```

**Does the HTML show three citations and a reference list with three entries? Any `?)`?**

Your answer:
